source.title: Deriving Neural Scaling Laws from the statistics of natural language
source.authors: Francesco Cagnetta; Allan Ravent'os; Surya Ganguli; M. Wyart

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: Measures held-out autoregressive loss as training-set size varies, using a power-law scaling analysis on new models and datasets. It tests data-limited scaling, not parameter- or compute-limited scaling.
record.gate_note: The paper reports data-limited loss scaling, scaling-collapse results, empirical fit intervals, and comparisons with exponents predicted from language statistics. It does not test small-run loss fits as predictions of much larger runs, compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, downstream tasks, or other modalities. Model-size checks are described, but no separate numerical outcomes are reported for them.
record.test_reason: The study trains GPT-2- and LLaMA-style models from scratch on TinyStories and WikiText subsets of about 1e5 to 1e8 tokens. It measures held-out autoregressive loss against training-set size, tuning hyperparameters and checking that larger models do not lower the loss. This is a direct test of data-limited power-law loss scaling (V1). The fitted exponents differ by dataset and drift with the fit window, which bears on V7. Parameter- and compute-limited scaling are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors conclude that two dataset statistics alone predict the data-limited loss exponent via αD = γ/(2β), with no free parameters: the decay of conditional entropy with context (γ) and the decay of token correlations with lag (β). The prediction matches GPT-2 and LLaMA learning curves on TinyStories and WikiText, and the n-gram curves collapse under the predicted rescaling. They note the tests reach only a few tens of tokens of effective horizon and academic data scales, so extension to industrial scales is open.
record.recipe_differences: The study derives data-limited predictions from measured language statistics and tests them on GPT-2- and LLaMA-style models, rather than reproducing the original broad parameter-, data-, and compute-scaling sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported results vary with dataset and fitting choices. The WikiText correlation decay is described as a broken power law and the authors use its short-lag exponent. The empirical loss-exponent intervals vary with the number of fitted points. For TinyStories LLaMA, the sharpest visual n-gram collapse uses β ≃ 0.65 rather than the independently measured β=0.88 ± 0.06. Context length T also limits the range over which the prediction is expected to hold.

fits_no_version.finding: The decay exponent of next-token conditional entropy with context length, γ, is consistent across GPT-2 APE, GPT-2 RoPE, LLaMA, Mamba and n-gram models for a given dataset.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dataset-level language statistics (entropy decay γ, correlation decay β) are architecture-independent and predict the data-limited exponent as αD = γ/(2β).

fits_no_version.finding: LLaMA's n-gram learning curves collapse best at β of about 0.65, below the measured 0.88 ± 0.06.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The quality of the n-gram learning-curve collapse can depend on architecture even when the loss exponent matches.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The authors say the tests cover a finite range: the largest effective horizon is a few tens of tokens, and the conclusions may not extend to industrial dataset and context scales. Hyperparameter search is not exhaustive, particularly for the largest datasets. The WikiText conditional-entropy exponent is estimated from only the first few converged points, and the study notes fitting-window and architecture sensitivity.
record.rows_left_out: No additional directly reported numerical autoregressive scaling-fit results were omitted. Figure-only curves for the reported model/dataset settings are recorded separately in R1-R5.

untested.parts: Parameter-limited and compute-limited scaling. Also data-limited scaling beyond about 1e8 tokens and beyond contexts of a few tens of effective tokens.
Not tested. The exponent is predicted from language statistics rather than extrapolated from small runs to larger ones.
Not tested: there is no controlled fixed-parameter comparison of depth or width.
Not tested: there are no other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning or transfer.
Not tested: no downstream tasks are measured.
Parameter-counting conventions, training schedules and compute-optimal split comparisons are not tested.

missing.what: Within-horizon n-gram excess losses decay with exponents δn above γ/(2β) for n ≤ 12 (GPT-2, TinyStories, T=128). This supports the fast-learning regime assumed behind the single power law.

Model-size checks: for each dataset size, larger GPT-2 (274M, 600M) and LLaMA sizes were tested and did not lower validation loss. This confirms the runs are data-limited, as V1 requires. No numbers are given.
Predicted exponents αD = 0.185 ± 0.013 (TinyStories) and 0.141 ± 0.025 (WikiText), against which the empirical fits are compared.

record.verdict_notes: The power law spans only about 1e5 to 1e8 tokens, roughly three decades. The empirical exponents (0.14-0.19) are much steeper than Kaplan's data-limited exponent of about 0.095, consistent with V7's dataset dependence, though the study does not frame it this way. Hyperparameter search was not exhaustive at the largest P. That could contribute to the downward drift of the exponent at large m.

versions.untested_parts: Tests data-limited loss versus training tokens only; does not test parameter- or compute-limited scaling.
No test of whether power laws fitted on small runs predict the losses of much larger runs.
No compute-budget sweep or loss-minimising parameter/token allocation.
Does not compare loss at fixed parameter count across depth, width, and architecture in a controlled way.
Experiments use text next-token prediction trained from scratch; no other modality, repeated-data, fine-tuning, or transfer regime is tested.
Tests sensitivity to dataset, architecture, and some fitting choices, but not parameter-count conventions, compute-optimal allocation, or broad training-schedule and data-source comparisons.

relationships.condition: GPT-2 (APE and RoPE) and LLaMA-style models, TinyStories and WikiText, P about 1e5 to 1e8 tokens, contexts large enough that n*(P) is much less than T
relationships.reason: Held-out loss falls as a single power law over roughly three decades of data across architectures and datasets. TinyStories fits are stable near 0.18-0.19 for m=5-8 (R1-R10, R14-R19).
relationships.display_finding: Held-out loss follows a single power law across roughly three decades of data, with TinyStories exponents stable near 0.18–0.19 for m=5–8.

relationships.condition: TinyStories at the largest P in the lower envelope, and small context lengths T
relationships.reason: The fitted exponent drifts down as later points are added (m=11-12: [0.157, 0.178] and [0.149, 0.175]). The authors say the power law breaks once n*(P) approaches T, so it holds only while context is not a bottleneck (R11-R13, R1).
relationships.display_finding: Adding later points shifted exponent intervals from [0.157, 0.178] to [0.149, 0.175], with scaling breaking as n*(P) approached context length.

relationships.condition: Empirical lower-envelope exponent fits on TinyStories and WikiText

relation.reason: The study measures loss scaling directly and compares fitted exponents across datasets and fit windows.

tranche.reason: The empirical test uses training-data sweeps and held-out autoregressive loss in the data-limited regime, matching the original empirical method and measure. The new theoretical derivation does not change that test.
